extracted.intended_audience: inventors and prospective patent applicants (general public)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for preparing and prosecuting a patent application (primarily US-focused), including required components, specification/§112 requirements, provisional vs. non‑provisional distinctions, prosecution process, international/PCT filing, costs, and timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification (US non‑provisional utility application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification: Including title, cross-references, technical field, background, summary, brief description of drawings, detailed description, abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification is a required component of a US non-provisional utility application and must contain those listed parts to describe the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims: At least one claim required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims define the scope of legal protection sought; a non-provisional utility application must include at least one claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings: Required where necessary for understanding (almost always for utility patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include drawings whenever they are necessary to understand the claimed invention; for many utility patents drawings are effectively required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath or Declaration
rubrics_metrics.description: Oath or Declaration: Inventor's declaration of inventorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formal statement by the inventor(s) is a required part of a US non-provisional application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information Disclosure Statement (IDS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information Disclosure Statement: List of known prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must disclose known relevant prior art to the patent office via an IDS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application Data Sheet
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contains applicant names, correspondence address, priority claim data, and other bibliographic information required by the office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification requirements under 35 U.S.C. §112
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must comply with 35 USC 112, which includes enablement, written description, best mode, and definiteness requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §112 sets statutory standards for the content and clarity of the specification; the page lists the principal sub-requirements (enablement, written description, best mode, definiteness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement: Enable a POSITA to make and use the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must teach enough for a person skilled in the art to practice the invention without undue experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description
rubrics_metrics.description: Written description: Show possession of the invention as claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disclosure must demonstrate that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention at the time of filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Best mode: Disclose the best mode contemplated by the inventor (no longer a basis for invalidity post-AIA but still required).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although failure to disclose best mode is no longer a basis for invalidating an issued patent after the AIA, the best mode disclosure is still a statutory requirement in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Definiteness: Particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must be sufficiently definite to inform the public of the bounds of the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional application (purpose and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisional application: A less formal filing that establishes a priority date for 12 months. It is not examined and never matures into a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventors typically file a provisional first to establish priority, then file a non-provisional within 12 months claiming that priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑provisional application (formal filing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-provisional application: The formal application that is examined and may mature into a patent. The 20-year patent term runs from the non-provisional filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A non-provisional is the examined filing that can result in an issued patent; filing date of the non-provisional is the starting point for patent term calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent prosecution process
rubrics_metrics.description: After filing, the application is examined by a patent examiner who determines whether the claims meet patentability requirements. The examiner issues office actions (typically rejecting some or all claims), and the applicant responds with arguments and/or amendments. This back-and-forth continues until the application is allowed or finally rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecution is an iterative process of office actions and applicant responses. Success depends on persuasive arguments, claim amendments, and meeting procedural requirements until allowance or final rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (examiner assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner determines whether the claims meet patentability requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes the examiner's role in assessing patentability but does not enumerate specific tests; in practice patent offices evaluate novelty, inventive step/non‑obviousness, and industrial applicability/usefulness among other requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT (Patent Cooperation Treaty) international filing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Cooperation Treaty allows an applicant to file a single international application that has effect in 150+ member countries. The PCT delays the requirement to file in individual countries by 30 months from the priority date, providing time for market evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a PCT application centralizes an international filing and buys time (typically up to 30 months) before national phase entries are required in individual countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign filing strategy (Paris Convention priority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Within 12 months of a US filing (Paris Convention), an applicant can file in foreign countries claiming priority back to the US filing. Common strategies: PCT filing within 12 months, then national phase entries; or direct filings in priority foreign countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategize foreign filings to preserve priority dates and manage costs—common approaches include PCT route or direct national filings within the 12‑month Paris Convention window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs
rubrics_metrics.description: A typical US utility patent application costs $10,000-$30,000 in attorney fees plus $400-$1,600 in USPTO fees through allowance. Foreign filings add $5,000-$15,000 per country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget expectations: domestic prosecution can be costly and foreign filings materially increase total costs per jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeline (expected prosecution durations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Average US patent prosecution: 22-24 months from filing to allowance, with significant variation by art unit (mechanical: ~18 months; software: ~28 months; biotech: ~36 months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect prosecution timelines to vary substantially by technology area and examiner/office workload.
